newsitem.title: USA: Dole challenges Clinton to another debate on economy.
newsitem.headline: Dole challenges Clinton to another debate on economy.

text.p: An invigorated Bob Dole came out of his final debate with President Bill Clinton ready for more action by challenging him to a third debate.

After his aggressive attack on alleged ethical abuses at the White House during the Wednesday night debate, Dole told reporters and later a boisterous rally at a convention centre that he wanted another debate.

"We are very excited," Dole told several thousands cheering cheering supporters. His aides said Dole was "pumped up by his performance", although Dole shrugged that "I don't know" when asked if he won.
"We ought to have one more debate," Dole told the rally, repeating his debate call for another encounter.

"In fact I challenge the president -- let's have one more debate and talk about the economy, Mr. President, and tell us the truth -- how bad it is, how many people are working in two jobs ... how many families with the husband and wife working just to make ends meet."
Dole originally wanted more than the two presidential debates but he and Clinton finally decided on the two that Clinton had held out for.

The former senator, far behind in polls, continued his attack on ethics within the Clinton administration, a new theme this week in the Dole struggle to catch up with Clinton with less than three weeks before the election.

"We're going to carry California on Nov. 5," Dole said. "And we're going to win the election," he continued. "To stop and think what President Clinton has done to California, we ought to win in a landslide."

Dole said Californians are beginning to listen. "They want leadership. They want integrity. They want public ethics practiced in the White House. They don't want me looking through your FBI files -- and I don't want you to look through mine either."

Dole plans to give a major speech on Thursday in Riverside, California, on immigration. The influx of illegal immigration is a major issue in this state and Dole backs a ballot initiative to curb state spending on education and other benefits for children of illegal immigrants.
He then carries his campaign to Albuquerqe, New Mexico, Denver, Wichita, Kansas, Louisville, Kentucky and Richmond, Virginia before returning to Washington on Saturday.

Dole received deafening cheers in his post-debate pep rally speech introduced by former President Gerald Ford, with whom Dole ran as Ford's running mate in 1976. Ford also was in the debate audience at the University of San Diego.
"The present occupant of the White House is neither a Ford nor a Lincoln," said Ford. "He is a convertible Dodge and he ought to be traded in.
"Dole will be a great president. He is a person with impeccable integrity and high ethical standards."
Dole's wife Elizabeth told reporters after the debate that she thought Dole's discussion of the tax cut he proposed and the economic issues hit home.
"I think he really connected with people and their problems," she said.
